source_read: PDF, pp. 739–753 (all 15 pages read; Tables 1–6 and Figure 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; online supplementary files not available in the PDF and not read)

claims.overstatement: 'A meta-analysis restricted to abstinent users found a reliable difference only for learning efficiency' does not match the primary results. Six of nine abilities had 95% CIs excluding zero: learning efficiency −0.47, visual-spatial −0.42, comprehension knowledge −0.43, retrieval fluency −0.32, processing speed −0.28, psychomotor speed −0.35. The authors' abstract reports all six as below controls. Learning efficiency is the only ability whose prediction interval excludes zero, whose heterogeneity is negligible, and which stays significant in both sensitivity analyses (Table 6) and after trim-and-fill. If that is what 'reliable' means, the claim should say so, e.g. 'the only difference that was consistent across studies and robust to sensitivity analyses'. The magnitude line (no reliable difference in fluid reasoning, short-term working memory or reaction speed) is accurate.
claims.note: Numbers checked against Table 2 (p. 745): learning efficiency g −0.47 (95% CI −0.58 to −0.37), PI −0.60 to −0.34, 17 studies; fluid reasoning −0.02 (−0.46 to 0.42); short-term working memory −0.19 (−0.44 to 0.06); reaction and decision speed 0.00 (3 studies, no usable CI). 31 studies, 1008 abstinent users vs 984 controls (p. 744). Mean abstinence 128.8 days (SD 99.5) supports 'first months'. Education: users 12.31 vs controls 13.88 years, but only 48% of studies did not match groups on education (p. 744). This source therefore gives 'about half' rather than 'most'; the 'most' wording rests on Scott et al. (76%). Publication bias: Egger significant for short-term working memory (t=2.19, p=.05) and learning efficiency (t=2.76, p=.01). Trim-and-fill gives −0.04 and −0.40 respectively (p. 745), which supports 'some evidence of publication bias'.

anchors.locator: Results › Study Selection and Characteristics; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 31 studies; 1008 abstinent users and 984 healthy controls. Weighted age 33.41 vs 34.76; education 12.31 (SD .91) vs 13.88 (SD 1.43) years; mean abstinence 128.8 days (SD 99.5), 31 studies; mean duration of use 144 months.

Hedges' g (negative = users worse), 95% CI, prediction interval: learning efficiency −0.47 [−0.58, −0.37], PI [−0.60, −0.34], k=17, I² 1%; visual-spatial −0.42 [−0.74, −0.11], PI [−1.39, 0.54], k=5; comprehension knowledge −0.43 [−0.69, −0.18], PI [−1.32, 0.44]; retrieval fluency −0.32 [−0.59, −0.04]; processing speed −0.28 [−0.52, −0.04], PI [−1.34, 0.78], k=22; psychomotor −0.35 [−0.65, −0.05]; fluid reasoning −0.02 [−0.46, 0.42]; short-term working memory −0.19 [−0.44, 0.06]; reaction/decision speed 0.00 (k=3).

Removing high-risk-of-bias studies: learning efficiency −0.457 [−0.699, −0.246]; visual-spatial and comprehension knowledge intervals now include zero; short-term working memory −0.283 [−0.524, −0.042]. Removing the 4 abuse-or-dependence studies: only learning efficiency remains clearly below zero (−0.452 [−0.565, −0.340]).
Egger's test suggested bias for short-term working memory (t=2.19, df=10, p=.05) and learning efficiency (t=2.76, df=15, p=.01); trim-and-fill: −0.04 [−0.26, 0.18] and −0.40 [−0.52, −0.28].
48% of the studies did not match users and controls on education; educational discrepancy did not predict effect size in any ability tested.

claims.overstatement: 'Length of abstinence did not moderate the size of group differences' holds for 4 of the 5 abilities tested here but not for comprehension knowledge. There, length of abstinence was a significant moderator (Q model 27.58, p<.001, surviving Holm–Bonferroni within and across abilities). The printed coefficient (−0.00) and its interval (0.0002 to −0.0008, bounds reversed) do not allow the direction to be read. Suggest 'did not moderate the differences in most domains tested'.
claims.note: The second half of the sentence ('few studies tested people abstinent for more than a year') is consistent with the mean abstinence of 128.8 days (SD 99.5) across 31 studies, though the paper does not count studies over a year.

claims.note: The authors state the causal question cannot be answered from cross-sectional designs and that strong statements are premature. Their abstract also speaks of 'sequelae that persist beyond a period of abstinence', which presupposes the causal reading they then disclaim. That is an interpretation issue in the source, not a problem for the claim.

anchors.extracted: Authors cannot tell whether use leads to long-term impairment or whether pre-existing deficits are vulnerability factors, or both; strong statements about impaired cognition in abstinent users are premature.

Only cross-sectional designs available; no premorbid ability measures; education (12.3 vs 13.9 years) used as a partial proxy and may itself be affected by early use; premorbid inhibitory-control and personality differences may precede use; longitudinal studies of people before use are needed.

Confounders (quantity, route, other drugs, personality, comorbid disorders) insufficiently reported, so group differences may reflect uncontrolled variables; twin designs suggested; retained participants may be healthier than dropouts.

key_findings.correction: Inference is from p. 743 (excluding unclear-risk studies would have removed all studies) and Figure 1 (p. 748: index tests almost entirely unclear).
Units are uncertain: Table 1 gives duration of use in months, while the Discussion reads β=−0.16 as per year (p. 747).

reporting_issues.note: The text on high-risk-of-bias removal also says the results did not change (p. 745), while Table 6 shows visual-spatial and comprehension knowledge losing significance and short-term working memory gaining it (−0.283, −0.524 to −0.042).
Table 2 also gives Q=0.000 and I²=0 for three studies with g exactly 0.00, which suggests the three effect sizes were identical or imputed as zero; not explained.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 low confidence agreed; no funding or conflict statement found anywhere in the article.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed for the main conclusion. Add: the abstract's 'sequelae that persist beyond a period of abstinence' is causal and persistence wording for cross-sectional data. The text also says both sensitivity analyses 'did not change the results' (p. 745) although Table 6 shows several abilities changing significance.

missed: Length of abstinence significantly moderated the comprehension-knowledge difference (Q model 27.58, p<.001; survives Holm–Bonferroni), the only ability where it did (pp. 744, 746). This bears directly on the encyclopedia's statement that abstinence did not moderate group differences, and the card mentions it only as a printing error in the interval.

The primary analysis found six abilities with intervals excluding zero (Table 2, p. 745). The encyclopedia's 'reliable difference only for learning efficiency' needs the card to state the criterion (prediction interval, sensitivity analyses) so the claim can cite it.

The education effect size d=1.31 (p. 744) appears to use the standard deviations of study means (0.91 and 1.43 years), not participant-level SDs, so it should not be read as the size of the individual-level education gap.
Short-term working memory became significant once high-risk studies were removed (Table 6, p. 747), the opposite direction of change to the other abilities.
